power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Crossing initiation is delayed in virtual environments relative to a real test track, and effects observed in simulators can be absent on the track 33, so neither the absolute latencies to step-off nor necessarily their pattern may generalize directly to real streets; differences between age groups, however, were reproduced in both a CAVE simulator and a head-mounted display for most crossing measures 34, and conventional orientation and mobility assessment is itself imperfectly standardized 35 . The ex-Gaussian fits pooled two trials per participant at each pair of levels, far fewer than are typically used for such fits; τ therefore describes the group distribution and cannot distinguish long slow tails of the latency distribution within individuals from consistently slower participants, and the goodness-of-fit test, computed on the same trials, is anticonservative. With 9, 10 and 17 sessions per condition, the between-condition comparisons had limited statistical power. Among the 14 participants with SPVI whose acuity was recorded, acuity was concentrated between 1.0 and 1.6 logMAR (10 of 14; Table 1), too narrow a range to test whether the effects varied with acuity; in an exploratory analysis, acuity was not significantly correlated with latency to step-off (geometric mean per participant), Spearman r(12) = 0.27, p = 0.347. Head yaw is not equivalent to gaze direction. The virtual environment posed no physical risk; and the complexity levels were presented in a fixed order, so their effects are confounded with practice. Whether head-yaw kinematics predict travel incidents outside the laboratory remains to be determined in prospective studies.

text.text: Pedestrian injuries are most severe at uncontrolled crossings.
At a virtual crossing without tactile and auditory cues, adults with severe-to-profound visual impairment took longer than sighted adults to step off the curb.
Time spent at the curb may inform orientation and mobility assessment and accessible crossing design.

Pedestrians account for an increasing proportion of traffic fatalities in the United States 1.
text.formatted: Pedestrians account for an increasing proportion of traffic fatalities in the United States <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1</ref>.

text.text: Pedestrians struck at non-signalized crossings sustain more severe injuries and have higher mortality than those struck at signalized crossings 2 .
text.formatted: Pedestrians struck at non-signalized crossings sustain more severe injuries and have higher mortality than those struck at signalized crossings <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2</ref> .

text.text: At an uncontrolled crossing, no signal is available, and the decision to initiate crossing depends entirely on the pedestrian's own assessment of the traffic.
Severe vision loss is associated with a greater risk of death from unintentional injury 3.
text.formatted: Severe vision loss is associated with a greater risk of death from unintentional injury <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3</ref>.

text.text: For example, pedestrians with severe peripheral field loss identify fewer crossable gaps and more often accept gaps that are too short 4 .
text.formatted: For example, pedestrians with severe peripheral field loss identify fewer crossable gaps and more often accept gaps that are too short <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> .

text.text: However, pedestrians with low vision who travel independently judge crossing gaps as accurately as normally sighted pedestrians; without visual cues, both groups judge them less accurately 5 .
text.formatted: However, pedestrians with low vision who travel independently judge crossing gaps as accurately as normally sighted pedestrians; without visual cues, both groups judge them less accurately <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5</ref> .

text.text: These findings can be reconciled if vision loss limits the acquisition of gap information rather than its evaluation.
This question remains unresolved in people with severe-to-profound visual impairment (SPVI), whose residual vision is limited and, in ultra-low vision, rudimentary at best 6 .
text.formatted: This question remains unresolved in people with severe-to-profound visual impairment (SPVI), whose residual vision is limited and, in ultra-low vision, rudimentary at best <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6</ref> .

text.text: Yet in this population, mobility is among the activities for which people report benefiting from their residual vision 7 .
text.formatted: Yet in this population, mobility is among the activities for which people report benefiting from their residual vision <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7</ref> .

text.text: The open question is therefore not whether crossing outcomes differ with vision loss, but how the information required for crossing is acquired.
Orientation and mobility training teaches pedestrians with low vision to look in both directions before entering the roadway.
If degraded vision provides less information per look, visually impaired pedestrians would be expected to scan more.

The clearest evidence of compensatory scanning comes from homonymous hemianopia, in which pedestrians scan farther and more often toward the blind than toward the seeing hemifield 8 ; in a driving simulator, early large head scans toward the blind hemifield were associated with earlier fixation of, and faster responses to, hazards on that side 9 .
text.formatted: The clearest evidence of compensatory scanning comes from homonymous hemianopia, in which pedestrians scan farther and more often toward the blind than toward the seeing hemifield <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8</ref> ; in a driving simulator, early large head scans toward the blind hemifield were associated with earlier fixation of, and faster responses to, hazards on that side <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9</ref> .

text.text: Hemianopia, however, is a special case, because visual acuity is typically good and there is a defined direction toward which to compensate.

Without such a direction, the prediction is not supported: pedestrians with age-related macular degeneration, for instance, turn their heads less often than normally sighted pedestrians at a real intersection 10 .
text.formatted: Without such a direction, the prediction is not supported: pedestrians with age-related macular degeneration, for instance, turn their heads less often than normally sighted pedestrians at a real intersection <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10</ref> .

text.text: In laboratory gaze tasks, people with early to moderate retinitis pigmentosa increased head movement at the expense of eye movement, without increasing total gaze movement 11 .
text.formatted: In laboratory gaze tasks, people with early to moderate retinitis pigmentosa increased head movement at the expense of eye movement, without increasing total gaze movement <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11</ref> .

text.text: Even in hemianopia, the evidence is inconsistent: a virtual street-crossing study comparing clinical, simulated and absent hemianopia found no group differences in scanning behavior 12 .
text.formatted: Even in hemianopia, the evidence is inconsistent: a virtual street-crossing study comparing clinical, simulated and absent hemianopia found no group differences in scanning behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12</ref> .

text.text: Importantly, none of these studies examined street crossing at the severe end of visual impairment; in the one that included late-stage retinitis pigmentosa, these participants made minimal gaze movements 11 .
text.formatted: Importantly, none of these studies examined street crossing at the severe end of visual impairment; in the one that included late-stage retinitis pigmentosa, these participants made minimal gaze movements <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11</ref> .

text.text: Head and eye movements have been recorded in a headmounted display while patients with central, peripheral or combined impairment detected approaching vehicles and identified safe crossing opportunities in a virtual street 13 .
text.formatted: Head and eye movements have been recorded in a headmounted display while patients with central, peripheral or combined impairment detected approaching vehicles and identified safe crossing opportunities in a virtual street <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13</ref> .

text.text: In the combined-loss subgroup of that study, the group closest to SPVI, head turns were less frequent than in controls.
Because those participants judged a recorded scene while stationary, continuous head-yaw kinematics have not been measured while people with clinical SPVI physically cross a street.
Crossing is a decision made under uncertainty: the pedestrian accumulates information about approaching vehicles and initiates crossing when it is judged safe.

Models of decision making predict that the duration of this decision depends both on the rate at which visual information about approaching vehicles is acquired and on the amount of that information required before committing [14] [15] [16] .
text.formatted: Models of decision making predict that the duration of this decision depends both on the rate at which visual information about approaching vehicles is acquired and on the amount of that information required before committing <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref> .

text.text: The time spent at the curb, and its distribution across crossings, may therefore indicate the consequences of degraded vision.
To test this, we compared normally sighted adults, the same adults under simulated SPVI, and adults with clinical SPVI as they crossed a virtual street at graded levels of environmental complexity.
The simulation separated the immediate effect of acuity loss from adaptation, orientation and mobility training, and the habits that accompany long-standing vision loss.
Because participants completed every crossing, measures of head scanning and of the time spent at the curb characterize how a crossing was approached, not whether the decision was safe.
We asked whether people with severe vision loss compensate by increasing head scanning or by spending more time at the curb.
Twenty-seven adults participated: 10 normally sighted controls and 17 participants with SPVI (Table 1), all recruited from the Johns Hopkins Department of Ophthalmology.
text.formatted: Twenty-seven adults participated: 10 normally sighted controls and 17 participants with SPVI (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>), all recruited from the Johns Hopkins Department of Ophthalmology.

text.text: SPVI was defined as visual acuity of 20/200 (1.0 logMAR) or worse, spanning the severe (20/200-20/400) and profound (worse than 20/400, including near-total) categories of the International Classification of Diseases, Ninth Revision, Clinical Modification; the profound category corresponds broadly to ultra-low vision 7 , for which orientation and mobility assessments have been developed for vision-restoration trials 17 .
text.formatted: SPVI was defined as visual acuity of 20/200 (1.0 logMAR) or worse, spanning the severe (20/200-20/400) and profound (worse than 20/400, including near-total) categories of the International Classification of Diseases, Ninth Revision, Clinical Modification; the profound category corresponds broadly to ultra-low vision <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7</ref> , for which orientation and mobility assessments have been developed for vision-restoration trials <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17</ref> .

text.text: Acuity was estimated with the Berkeley Rudimentary Vision Test 18 .
text.formatted: Acuity was estimated with the Berkeley Rudimentary Vision Test <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18</ref> .

text.text: Controls had no ocular disease or surgery and an acuity of 20/25 (0.1 logMAR) or better in each eye.
We excluded participants with self-reported cognitive, hearing, or mobility impairment, and participants wore their habitual correction.

text.text: Participants with SPVI completed the protocol with and without a long cane; only trials without a mobility aid (cane or guide dog) were analyzed.

The virtual environment was developed in Unity and presented on an HTC VIVE Pro Eye head-mounted display (HTC Corporation, New Taipei City, Taiwan; 1440 × 1600 pixels per eye, 110° diagonal field of view, 90 Hz), with head pose tracked in six degrees of freedom by external base stations.
Participants physically walked each crossing in the tracked laboratory space (Figure 1).

text.text: An experimenter walked beside the participant in every trial.
No auditory or tactile traffic information was provided; the only non-visual cue was a pair of wooden platforms on the floor at the positions of the two virtual curbs.
The environment consisted of a straight roadway with a curb on each side and a marked crosswalk (Figure 2).
text.formatted: The environment consisted of a straight roadway with a curb on each side and a marked crosswalk (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">2</ref>).

text.text: Each trial began with the participant standing on the near curb, facing the crosswalk.
Participants could view the scene for as long as they wished before crossing to a target on the opposite curb, approximately 4.6 m away.
At levels A and B, the street was oneway without a center line, and at levels C and D, it was two-way with a double yellow center line.

Level A was empty; level B contained parked cars and moving pedestrian avatars; level C contained moving vehicles in both directions that yielded at the crosswalk; and level D was level C with moving pedestrian avatars added.
For analyses of pairs of levels, levels A and B, which contained no moving vehicles, were grouped as low demand, and levels C and D, which contained moving vehicles, as high demand.
Street crossing was the first of three virtual environments in each session.
Levels were presented in a fixed order from A to D, so that every participant encountered the least demanding environment first.
Each level was preceded by an unrecorded practice trial.
Participants were instructed to cross at a comfortable speed and to avoid cars and pedestrians.
Each session contributed one crossing per level, for a total of 144 trials (NV 36, sSPVI 40, SPVI 68).
Head position (X along the crossing, Y vertical, Z lateral) and rotation were logged at approximately 9.1 Hz.
Of the three rotation angles, only yaw, the rotation about the vertical axis, was analyzed.

Yaw was referenced to 0° across the crosswalk, with positive values leftward, within -180° to 180°, and was not filtered; sessions that initialized facing the opposite direction (circular mean heading over the first 30 samples outside ±90°) were rotated by 180°.
Walking speed was computed as the horizontal (X-Z) displacement of the head between samples divided by the sampling interval, then smoothed with a 10-sample (approximately 1.1 s) moving average.
A guide-dog session for one participant with SPVI was excluded.
Where a level was recorded twice, the first recording that reached the far curb, at least 4.3 m from the start, was analyzed; the earlier recordings were a false start and an abandoned attempt.
Trials in which the participant reached the far curb and then moved back toward the start by more than 1 m were ended at the farthest point (three trials for one control participant).
Step-off was the first sample at which smoothed walking speed reached 0.3 m/s.
The pre-initiation epoch extended from trial onset to the preceding sample, and its duration was the latency to step-off.

Latency to step-off agreed with the latency detected by the curb step-down criterion of our recent work 20 (a head drop of at least 0.1 m within 0.5 m of the start) in the 136 trials in which a step-down was detected, with high correlation (Spearman r(134) = 0.87, Pearson r(134) = 0.98, both p < 0.001).

The walking bout was the first run of at least 25 consecutive samples (approximately 2.7 s) above 0.3 m/s.
We identified it in 139 of 144 trials (NV 36, sSPVI 40, SPVI 63), and reported its duration as walking-bout duration.
Cumulative absolute yaw and scanning rate.

The primary measure, cumulative absolute yaw (Ψ scan = Σ|Δψ|), was the sum of absolute sample-to-sample yaw changes, each wrapped to ±180°, computed over the whole trial, the pre-initiation epoch and the walking bout (Figure 3).

text.text: Cumulative absolute yaw quantifies the total angular excursion of the head irrespective of direction; a 40° turn to the left and then back, for example, contributes 80°.
Scanning rate (°/s) was Ψ scan divided by the duration of the corresponding epoch (latency to stepoff or walking-bout duration).
Pre-post scanning index.

The division of head scanning between the pre-initiation epoch and the walking bout was quantified for each trial as (Ψ post -Ψ pre )/(Ψ post + Ψ pre ), which ranges from -1 (head scanning only in the pre-initiation epoch) to +1 (head scanning only in the walking bout).

Because both terms depend on the durations of the pre-initiation epoch and the walking bout, we computed a rate-normalized pre-post scanning index in the same way from the two scanning rates as a sensitivity analysis.

Of the two forms of compensation considered in the Introduction, only additional time at the curb was observed: participants with SPVI took longer to step off than normally sighted participants, whereas cumulative absolute head yaw did not differ significantly between SPVI and normal or simulated vision, either in the pre-initiation epoch or in the walking bout.

Because cumulative absolute head yaw accumulates with time, the additional time at the curb would by itself be expected to increase it; its smaller, non-significant increase in SPVI reflects a scanning rate that was, if anything, lower than under normal vision (Table 3, rows 5 and 11).

text.text: Across viewing conditions, head scanning was influenced more by environmental complexity than by vision.
The prediction that degraded vision requires more extensive head scanning was not supported at the severe end of vision loss.

Compensatory head and eye scanning presupposes sufficient residual form vision for directed head movements to be informative: it has been documented where a defined blind field provides a direction for head and eye scanning, as in hemianopia 8, 9 , and where a useful visual field remains, as in early to moderate retinitis pigmentosa, in which head movement increases at the expense of eye movement, whereas participants with late-stage disease made minimal gaze movements 11 .

text.text: With severely degraded vision, the available compensation may instead be additional time.

The absence of increased head scanning in SPVI is consistent with reduced or unchanged head turning in macular degeneration 10 , reduced eye scanning in retinitis pigmentosa with tunnel vision 26 , and fewer head turns in the combined-loss group closest to SPVI in a study in which patients, judging a recorded scene while stationary, also identified safe gaps later than controls 13 .

text.text: Together, these findings are consistent with the view that vision loss limits the acquisition of information rather than its evaluation, so that degraded input increases the time required; whether accuracy declines when that time is not available was not tested here.
The present analysis quantified the extent of head yaw, not its direction.

In clinical SPVI, the slow tail of the latency distribution was longer than under normal vision at both low and high demand, without a detectable shift of its peak, a dissociation that distributional analyses of response times are designed to detect 14 .

text.text: The fastest crossings in SPVI were therefore initiated almost as promptly as under normal vision, whereas most were delayed by a variable rather than a fixed amount.

In diffusion-model simulations of speeded two-choice decisions, poorer-quality evidence, expressed as a lower drift rate, results mainly in a larger τ; a longer non-decision time (sensory encoding and motor execution) results only in a larger μ; and greater caution, expressed as a wider decision boundary, results in a larger τ but also in a substantially larger μ 16,27 .

Of the two determinants of the time spent at the curb outlined in the Introduction, a longer slow tail of the latency distribution without a significant shift of its peak is therefore more consistent with slower acquisition of visual information about approaching vehicles than with a larger amount of information required before committing, although μ was imprecisely estimated under the participant-level bootstrap, ex-Gaussian parameters do not map uniquely onto diffusion-model parameters, and the two determinants cannot be fully separated without a measure of accuracy 16 .

text.text: The slow tail of the latency distribution was already longer at levels A and B, which contained no moving vehicles, so the effect of vision loss did not depend on traffic; at levels C and D, which contained moving vehicles, the slow tail of the latency distribution was significantly longer than at levels A and B only in SPVI, but this increase did not differ significantly between viewing conditions, so whether traffic adds to the effect of vision loss remains unresolved.
Two alternative explanations are also consistent with the data on latency to step-off.

Because the task provided no auditory or tactile traffic information and cane trials were excluded, prolonged latencies to step-off may reflect the absence of visual evidence about approaching vehicles rather than its slow accumulation.

In addition, the vehicles at levels C and D yielded, which makes these latencies to step-off incomparable with the gap-acceptance literature; because yielding is likely to be difficult to detect at this level of vision, part of the slow tail of the latency distribution may reflect the time taken to abandon the judgment of whether vehicles had yielded rather than to complete it.
Comparing simulated with clinical SPVI separates the immediate effect of acuity loss from adaptation to long-standing vision loss.

On mean latency to step-off, the sighted controls with the Bangerter filters showed most of the additional latency to step-off of clinical SPVI, and simulated and clinical SPVI did not differ significantly on any measure (Table 3, rows 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18 and 21); the additional latency to step-off therefore does not require long-standing vision loss.

text.text: Cumulative absolute head yaw in the pre-initiation epoch was also higher with the Bangerter filters but not in clinical SPVI; the increase with the filters may reflect a more conservative decision criterion under unfamiliar blur.

The smaller increase in cumulative absolute head yaw with complexity in the walking bout in SPVI, which was not observed under simulated SPVI, together with walking bouts that were no shorter than under normal vision, suggests that participants with long-standing vision loss made the decision to step off before initiating crossing and then crossed with little further visual updating of the traffic scene, whereas participants under the acute blur produced by the Bangerter filters continued to scan as sighted pedestrians do; neither difference was tested directly.

The slow tail of the latency distribution was longest in SPVI, although acuity with the Bangerter filters was poorer than that of 11 of the 14 participants with SPVI whose acuity was recorded (Table 1); any excess over simulation, if confirmed, would therefore reflect aspects of clinical SPVI that the Bangerter filters do not simulate, such as field loss, disease-specific visual characteristics and age, or strategies adapted to non-visual cues.

text.text: Computed from scanning rate, the pre-post scanning index did not change significantly, so the larger proportion reflects a longer pre-initiation epoch rather than a higher scanning rate at the curb relative to that during the walking bout: with moving vehicles, participants with SPVI spent longer at the curb, whereas walking bouts were not longer at higher complexity and their cumulative absolute head yaw in the walking bout increased only slightly.

text.text: The redistribution of head scanning toward the curb is therefore a consequence of the additional time at the curb rather than a separate form of compensation, consistent with a decision to step off that was completed before crossing was initiated.

The additional time at the curb could reflect slower acquisition of visual information about approaching vehicles or a larger amount of information required before committing, and the two have different implications.

If vision loss slows acquisition, as the present results suggest, instructing a patient or client to scan more would not be expected to help, whereas preserving time at the curb would; if it increases the amount of information required, the time spent at the curb reflects a strategy that may be amenable to training.

In either case, limited head movement at a curb does not by itself indicate that a patient or client is not surveying the street, and training environments could be graded by environmental complexity rather than by acuity.
Both remain hypotheses.

To our knowledge, no study has shown that increased head or eye scanning improves crossing safety in low vision; in drivers with hemianopia, auditory reminders increased early head scanning, and early scans were associated with faster responses to hazards in a simulator, but whether this improves safety has not been tested prospectively 9 .

text.text: Head yaw is not equivalent to gaze direction.
The virtual environment posed no physical risk; and the complexity levels were presented in a fixed order, so their effects are confounded with practice.
Whether head-yaw kinematics predict travel incidents outside the laboratory remains to be determined in prospective studies.

Pedestrians with SPVI took longer to step off than normally sighted pedestrians, and the additional time was variable and often long rather than fixed; they did not scan at a higher rate, so any increase in their cumulative head scanning resulted from the additional time.

When vehicles were moving, a larger share of their head scanning occurred before step-off, because they spent longer at the curb rather than because their scanning rate at the curb rose relative to that during walking.

For pedestrians with SPVI, the time spent at the curb, and its variable, rightskewed lengthening, may therefore be a more informative target than the extent of head scanning, both for orientation and mobility assessment and for the design of accessible crossings, particularly uncontrolled crossings at which no non-visual information about yielding vehicles is available.
